content: Etrasimod has not been studied in combination with antineoplastic, immune-modulating, or non-corticosteroid immunosuppressive therapies. Co-administration of etrasimod with such therapies should be avoided during and in the weeks following its administration. The concurrent use of etrasimod and mogamulizumab may enhance the immunosuppressive effects of each drug, increasing the risk of infection. Alternative therapies should be considered to avoid this interaction. Etrasimod and momelotinib, when used together, may amplify each other’s immunosuppressive effects, leading to an elevated risk of infection. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use alternative drugs. The combination of etrasimod and monomethyl fumarate has not been studied but may result in additive immunosuppressive effects, increasing the risk of infection. Avoid co-administration or consider alternative therapies. Etrasimod and mosunetuzumab may increase each other’s immunosuppressive effects, heightening the risk of infection. This combination should be avoided, or alternative drugs should be used. Etrasimod and motixafortide may have additive immunosuppressive effects, raising the risk of infection. Avoid co-administration or use alternative therapies. The concurrent use of etrasimod and moxetumomab pasudotox may lead to enhanced immunosuppressive effects, increasing the risk of infection. Alternative therapies should be considered to avoid this interaction. Etrasimod and muronomab-CD3 may interact through aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibition, potentially increasing immunosuppressive effects and the risk of infection. Avoid this combination or use alternative drugs. The combination of etrasimod and mycophenolate may result in additive immunosuppressive effects due to aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibition, increasing the risk of infection. Avoid co-administration or consider alternative therapies. Etrasimod and nadofara gene firadenovec may amplify each other’s immunosuppressive effects, leading to an elevated risk of infection. This combination should be avoided, or alternative drugs should be used. Etrasimod and nadolol may exhibit pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially causing transient decreases in heart rate and delays in AV conduction. While stable beta-blocker treatment with etrasimod has not shown additive effects on heart rate reduction, caution is advised when initiating beta-blocker therapy with stable etrasimod treatment or when combining it with other heart rate-reducing drugs. Modify therapy or monitor closely when these drugs are co-administered.
